transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Patel. It is good to see you back in the clinic for your follow-up.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm here. I hope this is a quick visit.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I want to start by looking at the incision on your arm to see how it's healing.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's fine. I'm more interested in why the visit in the ER was such a nightmare.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know that part of the experience was very difficult. There was an issue with how the procedure was handled.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: An issue? You mean the fact that I felt every single stitch?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Things didn't go quite right with the numbing process.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's a very vague way of saying I was in agony while you were sewing my skin. Did you not use the lidocaine?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We were really busy that night, and I am sorry for any confusion regarding the pain management.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Confusion? I told you it hurt. I explicitly told the staff it hurt. I felt like I was being ignored.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. But the important thing now is that the wound is closed and there is no infection.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care about the infection right now. I want to know why this happened. Was the equipment broken? Did you run out of medicine?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There was just some a lack of coordination in the moment.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That doesn't answer my question. Who was responsible for checking if I was numb?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's a complex environment in the ER. I'm sorry you felt that way.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I didn't feel that way, I was actually in pain. This is exactly why I don't trust the process here. You just brush it off with a general apology.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. Now, moving forward, I want to make sure we have a concrete plan for your recovery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm still not clear on what actually went wrong.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Like I said, there were some complications with the timing of the infiltration.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You still aren't saying it. Did you forget to check my pain level?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm sorry that the experience was unpleasant.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Unpleasant. That's a funny word for it.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Let's focus on the next steps so we can get you back to work. First, I'm going to schedule a suture removal for exactly seven days from today, which will be next Tuesday at 10:00 AM.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Fine.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: When you come in for that, you'll meet with the attending physician, Dr. Sarah Jenkins, who has already been briefed on your case. She will perform the final check and sign off on your discharge from the wound clinic.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Does she know about the pain?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, she is aware of the concerns. I have also entered a formal incident report into our quality safety system, which triggers a departmental review of our anaesthetic protocols for lacerations.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is that just for the record, or does it actually change something?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It initiates a mandatory review. In addition, I've created a note in your electronic chart specifically flagging your preference for a pre-procedure pain check for any future interventions you have at this facility.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'll believe that when I see it in the portal.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That's fair. You can check the "Patient Notes" section of your portal by tomorrow evening to verify that the flag is there. Also, if you notice any redness or if the site starts to feel warm before Tuesday, I want you to call my direct line—which I've written on this card—and we will move the appointment up to tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Why should I trust you'll actually listen next time?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The documentation I've put in now is the safeguard for your future visits. It ensures that any provider who sees you is alerted to this specific requirement.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'll read the notes. If they aren't there, I'm calling the patient advocate.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is your right, and I've provided the advocate's office number on the back of this card as well. Do you have any other questions about the suture removal schedule?

H.justification: The resident uses rushing language to pivot away from the patient's distress ('Now, moving forward', 'Let's focus on the next steps').

E.justification: The resident uses platitudes and hedging ('things didn't go quite right', 'lack of coordination', 'complications with the timing') without explicitly naming the error.

A.justification: Direct apologies are offered, but they are diluted by excuses regarding how busy the ER was and by framing the pain as 'confusion' or 'unpleasant'.

R.justification: The resident uses generic validation ('I understand', 'I hear you') but fails to name specific emotions or engage with the patient's emotional bids.

T.justification: The resident provides a specific timeline (Tuesday at 10:00 AM), a named patient role (checking the portal), and addresses prevention (incident report and chart flag).
